problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have solved the problem completely. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,2025\}\) such that the uncovered squares are \((i,\sigma(i))\) for \(i=1,\dots ,2025\).

2. **Notation for left/right parts of a row.**  
   For a fixed row \(i\) define  

   \[
   \ell_i:=\sigma(i)-1\qquad(\text{number of squares left of the uncovered one}),
   \qquad
   r_i:=2025-\sigma(i)\qquad(\text{number of squares right of it}).
   \]

   Then \(\ell_i+r_i=2024\) for every \(i\).  
   Because \(\sigma\) is a permutation, the multiset \(\{\ell_i\mid i=1,\dots ,2025\}\) equals \(\{0,1,\dots ,2024\}\); the same holds for \(\{r_i\}\).

3. **Lower bound (Lemma 1).**  
   *Lemma 1.* Any admissible tiling uses at least \(2\,(2025-1)=4048\) rectangles.  

   *Proof.*  
   Consider the **left part** of the board  

   \[
   L:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le2025,\;1\le j\le\ell_i\}.
   \]

   For each row with \(\ell_i>0\) the square \((i,\ell_i)\) is the **right‑most** square of that row’s left part.  
   Since the numbers \(\ell_i\) are all distinct, these right‑most squares lie in distinct columns.  

   Let a rectangle \(R\) of the tiling intersect \(L\). Because a rectangle is a Cartesian product of a set of consecutive rows and a set of consecutive columns, its right side is a vertical line at some column \(c\).  
   If \(R\) contained two different right‑most squares \((i,\ell_i)\) and \((j,\ell_j)\) with \(\ell_i\neq\ell_j\), then without loss of generality \(\ell_i<\ell_j\). The column interval of \(R\) would have to contain \(\ell_j\); consequently it would also contain column \(\ell_i+1=\sigma(i)\) in row \(i\). That square \((i,\sigma(i))\) is uncovered, contradicting the fact that a tile cannot cover an uncovered square. Hence **no rectangle can contain two distinct right‑most squares of \(L\)**.  

   Exactly one row has \(\ell_i=0\) (the row where \(\sigma(i)=1\)). Therefore at least \(2025-1\) rectangles are needed to cover all squares of \(L\).

   The same argument applied to the **right part**  

   \[
   R:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le2025,\;\sigma(i)+1\le j\le2025\}
   \]

   shows that at least another \(2025-1\) rectangles are required: the squares \((i,2025-r_i)\) (the left‑most squares of each right part) are all in distinct columns and cannot share a rectangle.  

   Moreover a rectangle that contains a right‑most square of \(L\) cannot also contain a left‑most square of \(R\), because that would force the rectangle to cover an uncovered square as argued above. Consequently the two lower bounds add up, giving  

   \[
   \#\text{rectangles}\ge (2025-1)+(2025-1)=4048.
   \qquad\blacksquare
   \]

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   Choose the permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) (the main diagonal).  

   * Left tiles: for each row \(i\) with \(i>1\) place the horizontal rectangle  

     \[
     T^{\text{L}}_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j\le i-1\},
     \]

     which covers the left part of that row.  

   * Right tiles: for each row \(i\) with \(i<2025\) place the horizontal rectangle  

     \[
     T^{\text{R}}_i=\{(i,j)\mid i+1\le j\le2025\},
     \]

     which covers the right part of that row.  

   The first row has no left tile, and the last row has no right tile. Hence we obtain exactly  

   \[
   (2025-1)+(2025-1)=4048
   \]

   tiles.  
   The tiles are pairwise disjoint (they lie in distinct rows, and in each row the left and right tile are separated by the uncovered diagonal square). Every unit square not on the diagonal belongs to exactly one tile, and each row and each column contains precisely its diagonal square as the unique uncovered cell.  

   Thus the construction satisfies all conditions with \(4048\) tiles.

5. **Conclusion.**  
   Lemma 1 gives a universal lower bound of \(4048\) tiles, and the explicit construction achieves this bound. Hence the minimum possible number of tiles is \(\boxed{4048}\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###  

Let  

\[
B=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n\},\qquad n=2025 .
\]

A *tiling* is a collection \(\mathcal{T}\) of axis‑parallel rectangles whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union is a subset of \(B\).  
The requirement “each row and each column has exactly one uncovered unit square’’ forces the set of uncovered squares to be  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\},
\]

where \(\sigma\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).  

For each row \(i\) put  

\[
\ell_i:=\sigma(i)-1,\qquad r_i:=n-\sigma(i).
\]

Thus \(\ell_i\) (resp. \(r_i\)) counts the squares to the left (resp. right) of the uncovered square in row \(i\).  
Since \(\sigma\) is a bijection,  

\[
\{\ell_i\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}=\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\},
\qquad
\{r_i\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}=\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1 (Lower bound)

*Statement.* Any tiling satisfying the condition uses at least \(2(n-1)\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  
Define the left part of the board  

\[
L:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j\le\ell_i\}.
\]

If \(\ell_i>0\) the square \((i,\ell_i)\) is the right‑most element of row \(i\) inside \(L\).  
By (1) the columns \(\ell_i\) are all distinct, so these squares lie in distinct columns.

Consider a rectangle \(R\in\mathcal{T}\) that meets \(L\).  
Let its column interval be \([c_{\min},c_{\max}]\).  
If \(R\) contained two distinct right‑most squares \((i,\ell_i)\) and \((j,\ell_j)\) with \(\ell_i<\ell_j\), then \(c_{\max}\ge\ell_j\). Consequently column \(\ell_i+1=\sigma(i)\) would also belong to the interval, and the square \((i,\sigma(i))\) (which is uncovered) would be covered by \(R\) – impossible. Hence **each rectangle can contain at most one right‑most square of \(L\)**.

Exactly one row has \(\ell_i=0\); all other \(n-1\) rows have \(\ell_i>0\). Therefore at least \(n-1\) rectangles are needed to cover all squares of \(L\).

An analogous argument applied to the right part  

\[
R:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;\sigma(i)+1\le j\le n\}
\]

shows that at least another \(n-1\) rectangles are required: the squares \((i,n-r_i)\) (the left‑most squares of each right part) are all in distinct columns and cannot share a rectangle.

Finally, a rectangle that contains a right‑most square of \(L\) cannot also contain a left‑most square of \(R\); otherwise its column interval would contain both \(\sigma(i)\) and \(\sigma(j)\) for some rows \(i,j\), forcing it to cover an uncovered square. Hence the two collections of rectangles are disjoint, and the lower bounds add:

\[
|\mathcal{T}|\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1).
\qquad\blacksquare
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Construction attaining the bound

Choose the permutation \(\sigma(i)=i\) (the main diagonal).  
For each row \(i\) with \(i>1\) place the horizontal rectangle  

\[
T^{\text{L}}_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j\le i-1\},
\]

and for each row \(i\) with \(i<n\) place  

\[
T^{\text{R}}_i=\{(i,j)\mid i+1\le j\le n\}.
\]

The first row has no left tile, the last row has no right tile.  
Thus the total number of tiles is  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1)=4048 .
\]

These tiles are pairwise disjoint (they occupy distinct rows, and in each row the left and right tile are separated by the uncovered diagonal square). Every unit square not on the diagonal belongs to exactly one tile, while the diagonal squares \((i,i)\) remain uncovered. Consequently each row and each column contains precisely one uncovered square.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Minimality

Lemma 1 shows that no admissible tiling can use fewer than \(4048\) rectangles, and the construction above uses exactly \(4048\) rectangles. Hence the lower bound is tight, and the minimal possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]
